live_plab_copy.pearl: HUS is a thrombotic microangiopathy: fragmented red cells on the blood film, low platelets and rising creatinine; some children need dialysis, so monitor counts and renal function closely.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: HUS triad: haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient presents with chronic cough, weight loss and night sweats, and pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected.

What is important?

options.A: Wait in the main waiting room and request a chest X-ray first
options.B: Start empirical quadruple therapy before any investigations
options.C: Isolate with airborne precautions and send sputum for AFB
options.D: Prescribe amoxicillin and review if the cough persists at 2 weeks
options.E: Request an interferon-gamma release assay and discharge home

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Isolate with airborne precautions and send sputum for AFB
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Chronic cough with weight loss and night sweats suggests pulmonary TB, so the patient should be isolated or masked, with infection-control precautions, and investigated with chest X-ray and sputum for acid-fast bacilli, culture and rapid molecular testing (NICE NG33).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. A shared waiting room risks airborne transmission to others. B. Samples should be obtained before treatment to confirm the diagnosis and drug sensitivities. D. Amoxicillin does not treat TB and may delay diagnosis. E. An IGRA does not diagnose active TB, and discharge without investigation risks progression and transmission.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Suspected pulmonary TB means two things at once: protect others with isolation or masking and airborne precautions, and confirm the diagnosis with sputum samples before treatment so sensitivities are known.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Chronic cough ↓ Weight loss and night sweats ↓ Suspected pulmonary TB ↓ Airborne transmission risk and need for microbiological confirmation ↓ Isolate and send sputum for AFB
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, empirical quadruple therapy first — treatment is eventually needed, but starting before sputum samples loses microbiological confirmation and drug-sensitivity data.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Suspected TB: isolate with airborne precautions and send sputum before starting treatment.

A 35-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. He feels well and asks why treatment is recommended despite having no symptoms.

What is the key reason?

options.A: Treatment is started once the CD4 count falls below 350
options.B: Treatment is mainly needed during opportunistic infections
options.C: HIV is often cleared by the immune system without treatment
options.D: A short antiretroviral course can eradicate HIV
options.E: Antiretrovirals suppress HIV and slow disease progression

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Antiretrovirals suppress HIV and slow disease progression
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Effective antiretroviral therapy suppresses viral replication, preserves immune function and reduces HIV-related morbidity.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Current guidance recommends treatment for all people with HIV regardless of CD4 count. B. HIV treatment is lifelong rather than limited to opportunistic infections. C. Untreated HIV does not clear spontaneously. D. Antiretroviral therapy suppresses but does not eradicate HIV.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Antiretroviral therapy is offered to everyone with HIV regardless of CD4 count; a sustained undetectable viral load preserves immunity and prevents sexual transmission.
live_plab_copy.thinking: New HIV diagnosis ↓ Asymptomatic but the virus is still replicating ↓ ART suppresses the virus and preserves CD4 cells ↓ Slows disease progression
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, start once CD4 falls below 350 — this reflects older practice, but treatment is now recommended for all, whatever the CD4 count.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Treat HIV at diagnosis, regardless of CD4 count or symptoms.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: HIV raises TB risk: test every TB patient for HIV.

options.C: Antibiotics can disrupt normal gut flora and promote C. difficile overgrowth
options.E: Antibiotics permanently eliminate all intestinal bacteria

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Antibiotics can disrupt normal gut flora and promote C. difficile overgrowth
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Antibiotic exposure can disrupt protective intestinal microbiota, allowing C. difficile to proliferate and produce toxins.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not cause appendicitis. B. They do not invariably cause inflammatory bowel disease. D. Antibiotics can themselves cause diarrhoea. E. They do not permanently eliminate all intestinal bacteria.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Antibiotic stewardship is central to C. difficile prevention; broad-spectrum agents such as clindamycin, cephalosporins and quinolones carry particular risk.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Normal gut flora resists C. difficile ↓ Antibiotics disrupt this protective microbiota ↓ C. difficile proliferates and produces toxin ↓ Antibiotics can disrupt normal gut flora and promote C. difficile overgrowth
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, antibiotics permanently eliminate all intestinal bacteria — close to the truth but overstated: the flora is disrupted, not permanently wiped out.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Antibiotics disrupt protective gut flora; stewardship prevents C. difficile.

A patient develops diarrhoea during a hospital admission. Several other patients on the ward have recently developed similar symptoms.

Which infection-control measure is particularly important when C. difficile is suspected?

options.A: Prophylactic oral vancomycin for contacts on the ward
options.C: Alcohol hand gel as the main hand hygiene method

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Contact isolation with sporicidal cleaning
live_plab_copy.why_correct: C. difficile can spread through spores, so appropriate isolation/contact precautions and effective environmental cleaning are important.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Prophylactic treatment of asymptomatic contacts is not recommended. C. Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores; soap-and-water hand washing is required. D. Unrestricted movement may facilitate transmission. E. Detergent alone does not reliably remove spores; chlorine-based or other sporicidal cleaning is needed.
live_plab_copy.pearl: C. difficile spores survive alcohol gel and detergent cleaning; isolate the patient promptly, use gloves and aprons, wash hands with soap and water, and clean with a chlorine-based agent.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Diarrhoea in hospital ↓ several patients affected = possible outbreak ↓ C. difficile forms resistant spores ↓ contact isolation plus sporicidal cleaning
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, alcohol hand gel as the main method — standard hand hygiene for many ward organisms, but it does not kill C. difficile spores; soap and water is needed.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: C. difficile: isolate, wash hands with soap and water, use sporicidal cleaning.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Rice-water stools in a traveller: cholera; rehydrate urgently.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Suspected HSV encephalitis = start IV aciclovir empirically and urgently.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient has fever and suspected bloodstream infection. Why should blood cultures be collected using careful aseptic technique?

options.A: To prevent the patient developing bacteraemia
options.B: To reduce contamination and false-positive results
options.C: To increase the sensitivity for detecting fungi
options.D: To allow antibiotics to be started before sampling
options.E: To reduce the volume of blood needed per bottle

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. To reduce contamination and false-positive results
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Contaminated blood cultures can lead to misleading results, unnecessary antibiotics and additional investigations.

Cultures should ideally be taken before antibiotics; asepsis does not alter this. E. Adequate blood volume is still required.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Take blood cultures with skin antisepsis and aseptic technique, ideally before antibiotics; skin contaminants such as coagulase-negative staphylococci cause false positives.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Suspected bloodstream infection ↓ Skin flora can enter the sample ↓ Contamination gives false positives ↓ Aseptic technique reduces this
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, to prevent bacteraemia — asepsis does protect patients during procedures, but in blood culture sampling its main purpose is an accurate, uncontaminated result.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Aseptic blood culture technique prevents contamination and misleading results.

A patient is strongly suspected of having bacterial meningitis.

What is the key principle?

options.A: Perform lumbar puncture before giving any antibiotics
options.B: Obtain a CT head in all patients before treatment
options.C: Start antibiotics once a petechial rash appears
options.D: Give oral antibiotics and review in 24 hours
options.E: Do not let investigations delay antibiotics

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Do not let investigations delay antibiotics
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Suspected bacterial meningitis requires urgent parenteral antibiotics; investigations such as LP or imaging should not delay treatment, especially when LP is contraindicated (NICE NG240).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. LP should not delay antibiotics and may be contraindicated in some patients. B. Imaging must not delay antibiotics. C. A rash is not always present, and treatment must not wait for one. D. Bacterial meningitis needs urgent parenteral antibiotics, not oral treatment with delayed review.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In suspected bacterial meningitis, give parenteral antibiotics without delay; lumbar puncture and imaging must never hold up treatment. Take blood cultures if this does not delay the first dose.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Strongly suspected bacterial meningitis ↓ Delay to treatment worsens outcome ↓ LP or CT can take time or be contraindicated ↓ Do not let investigations delay antibiotics
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, LP before any antibiotics — tempting because CSF gives the best microbiology. LP may be delayed or contraindicated; antibiotics come first, with cultures taken alongside.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Suspected bacterial meningitis: antibiotics first; investigations must not delay them.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Stable suspected endocarditis: several blood culture sets before antibiotics to find the organism.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, midstream urine for microscopy and culture — a routine infection screen, but it does not identify the organism infecting the heart valve.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Suspected endocarditis: multiple blood cultures before antibiotics.

akt_source.why_correct: Painless flesh-coloured genital growths are characteristic of anogenital warts caused by human papillomavirus.
akt_source.why_wrong: A. Primary syphilis typically causes a painless ulcer rather than multiple growths. C. PID causes pelvic pain, fever and cervical motion tenderness rather than external genital growths. D. Candidiasis causes itching and discharge. E. Herpes causes painful vesicles and ulcers.

A patient has a painless genital ulcer suspicious for syphilis.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Refer to sexual health for syphilis testing
options.B: Swab for herpes and start aciclovir without further tests
options.C: Prescribe topical antifungal cream and review in 2 weeks
options.D: Prescribe a topical steroid and review if not healing
options.E: Arrange biopsy via routine dermatology referral

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Refer to sexual health for syphilis testing
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A painless genital ulcer suggests primary syphilis, which should be assessed in a sexual health service with appropriate testing (such as dark-ground microscopy or PCR and serology), plus screening for other STIs (BASHH).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Herpes ulcers are typically painful, and treating for herpes without syphilis testing risks missing syphilis. C. An antifungal cream does not treat syphilis and delays diagnosis. D. A topical steroid without diagnosis is inappropriate and may delay treatment. E. A suspected syphilitic ulcer needs sexual-health assessment and testing, not routine dermatology biopsy.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A painless genital ulcer should be treated as possible primary syphilis; refer to sexual health for specific testing, a full STI screen and partner notification.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Genital ulcer ↓ Painless rather than painful ↓ Suggests primary syphilis ↓ Needs specific testing and STI screening ↓ Refer to sexual health for syphilis testing
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, swab for herpes and start aciclovir — herpes is a common cause of genital ulcers, but herpetic ulcers are typically painful and empirical aciclovir risks missing syphilis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Painless genital ulcer: think syphilis and refer to sexual health.
